title: The camel's choice
hook: every family wants him as guest, and he lets the camel choose, and it kneels near Abu Ayyub's house (sirah)

segments.voice: Yesterday, a mosque at Quba and a Friday prayer on the road, al-jumu'ah. Your line was: the first friday. Did a gathering make it onto your calendar? Day seven hundred seventy-one.

Who gets the guest? That is the question in the streets of Yathrib as the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, rides in. The city has invited him. Now household after household along the way wants him under its own roof. In Ibn Ishaq's sirah, one clan after another steps out and takes hold of the camel's rein: stay with us, we have numbers, we have strength, we will protect you. Any answer he gives will honor one family and pass over the rest, on his very first day. Today: the camel's choice.
screen: `WHO GETS THE GUEST?` → `HANDS ON THE REIN.` → `EVERY ANSWER PASSES SOMEONE OVER.`

segments.voice: His answer, as Ibn Ishaq tells it, is gentle and simple. Let her go her way, he says of the camel, for she is under command. So the rein is let go, and the camel walks on through the town with everyone watching. Bukhari picks up the scene from there. The camel kneels at a spot in the city, an open place where dates were spread out to dry, belonging to two orphan boys. And the Prophet says: this, if Allah wills, is the place to stay. Then he does something careful. He calls the two boys and asks to buy the land for a mosque. They say, in effect: no, we'll give it to you. He refuses the gift and pays for it. On that ground the mosque of Medina is built, and in the meantime he lodges nearby, in the house of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari. Muslim's collection preserves a small scene from those days: Abu Ayyub, living upstairs, can't bear to walk above the Prophet's head, and asks him to move to the upper floor. Consider what the camel spared everyone. No clan could say: he chose them over us. No one had to win. The choice was left to the camel, which, in his words, was under command, and he passed over no family himself. Then see what happened next: once the place was found, he didn't just take it. He paid two orphans what it was worth. Letting go of choosing did not mean letting go of care.
screen: `LET HER GO, SHE IS UNDER COMMAND.` · `THE CAMEL KNEELS.` · `HE PAYS THE TWO ORPHANS.` · `NO CLAN PASSED OVER.` · then, large: `LET THE CAMEL CHOOSE.`

segments.voice: The practice: let go of choosing once. Settle, and breathe. Think of a small decision on your plate today where several good options are tugging at you, and where it doesn't much matter which one wins. Where to eat, which friend to call first, which task to start. Notice your hands on the rein. Now loosen them. Decide that today you'll let something else choose: the first one that comes along, the one someone else prefers, the one that's nearest. If you pray, you can hand the choice to Allah. Feel your grip ease. The bell holds the time.
The camel's choice. Asked by clan after clan to stay with them, the Prophet let his camel walk free, and where she knelt became the place of the mosque in Medina. Today's word.
Your line: let the camel choose. Today, hand one small choice away, and see whose feelings it spares. Day seven hundred seventy-one.

screen: `DAY 771 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE PEOPLE OF THE BENCH.`

howItsDone: Muslims retell the camel's kneeling from the sirah and Sahih al-Bukhari when speaking of the founding of the Prophet's Mosque in Medina, and honor Abu Ayyub al-Ansari as his host.

fork.setup: you've arrived in a new city. every family is pulling your camel's rein, begging you to stay with them. what do you do?
options: stay with the most powerful clan.
let the camel walk, and stay where she kneels.
stay one night with each family in turn.
fork.reveal: in Ibn Ishaq he says let her go, she is under command; Bukhari says she knelt on the orphans' land, and he bought it for the mosque.

original.note: Arabic: 'under command', what the sirah has him say of the camel.

trapdoor: what you thought: a cute story about a camel picking a house.
what it means: handing the choice away kept any clan from being passed over on his first day.
what a scholar hears: Ibn Ishaq for 'she is under command'; Bukhari 3906 for the kneeling and the purchase from two orphans; Muslim for Abu Ayyub's upper floor.

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (the clans take the rein; 'let her go her way, for she is under command')
Sahih al-Bukhari 3906 (the camel kneels at the drying place of two orphans; 'this, if Allah wills, is the place'; he buys the land)
Sahih Muslim 2053 (Abu Ayyub's house; the upper floor)

notes: Bukhari 3906 and Muslim 2053 numbers cited from memory; confirm.
'She is under command' (ma'murah) is from Ibn Ishaq; confirm wording and that it should not be attributed to Bukhari.
Index hook says the camel kneels 'near Abu Ayyub's house'; Bukhari puts it on the orphans' land, with Abu Ayyub's house nearby. Script gives both. Confirm.
The orphans are named Sahl and Suhayl in Bukhari; names left out of the script for brevity.
Audit pass: 'handed to something with no stake in it' recast the Prophet's own reason ('she is under command') in the narrator's terms; the teach now gives his words.

Editor pass: 'every household' and 'asked by every clan' became 'household after household' and 'clan after clan', matching Ibn Ishaq's one-after-another telling; cut 'the community's first day began without a grudge' (an unsupported claim) for 'no family was passed over'; varied the 'look at' openers.
